note: Wisdom is paraphrased from the sources named, not quoted. Recipes are original and based on foods described in Norse and Germanic sources; they are modern adaptations.

wisdom.speaker: Hávamál, the Sayings of the High One
wisdom.era: Old Norse poem, recorded in the 13th century
wisdom.text: Cattle die and kinsfolk die, and you will die too. Only one thing never dies: the good name a person leaves behind.

wisdom.speaker: Hávamál, on the threshold
wisdom.text: Before you walk through a gate, look carefully around you, because you cannot know where an enemy may be waiting. Care at the door protects the whole household.

source.title: Bellows, The Poetic Edda (Hávamál, opening stanzas)

wisdom.speaker: Tacitus, Germania
wisdom.era: Roman historian, c. 98 CE, writing about the Germanic peoples
wisdom.text: He describes warriors who fought alongside their chief. To survive a chief who fell in battle brought lasting shame, and the companions fought to protect him.

recipes.name: Honey mead
recipes.history: Honey drinks are named throughout the Norse and Germanic sources, served at feasts and in the hall. This is a simple modern version, not a reconstruction of a specific brew.
steps: Warm 1 quart of the water and stir in the honey until it dissolves.
Add the rest of the water and let the mixture cool to about 75°F (24°C).
Pour into a sanitized fermenting vessel, stir in the nutrient, and add the yeast.
Fit an airlock and keep at room temperature for 3 to 6 weeks, until bubbling stops.
Siphon off the clear liquid, leaving the sediment behind, then bottle.
Store bottles upright for two weeks before drinking. Mead can be aged for months.
recipes.safety: Fermentation produces gas, so use an airlock and never seal a fermenting batch tightly. Clean all equipment well to prevent spoilage. Serve only to adults, and drink responsibly.

recipes.name: Slow-roasted boar or pork shoulder
recipes.history: In the Prose Edda, the cook of the feast in Valhalla prepares a boar named Sæhrímnir each evening, and it is whole again the next morning. Roasted meat was the centre of a Germanic feast, and this recipe follows that tradition.
ingredients: 3 lb (1.4 kg) boneless boar or pork shoulder
steps: Rub the meat with salt, juniper and garlic. Slip the garlic into small cuts in the meat.
Place in a heavy pan or roasting dish, brush with honey, and pour the ale or water around it.
Cover and roast for about 3 hours, until the meat is very tender and reaches 195°F (90°C).
Rest for 15 minutes, then slice or pull the meat and serve with the juices.
recipes.safety: Cook pork and boar until the centre reaches at least 145°F (63°C), and use 195°F (90°C) for a shoulder that you want to pull apart. Refrigerate leftovers within two hours.

recipes.name: Barley and wheat flatbread
recipes.history: Flat breads baked on a hot stone or griddle were a common, simple bread across northern Europe, and cereals such as barley were grown in the Norse world. This is a modern recipe in that style.
steps: Mix the flours and salt in a bowl.
Stir in the water until a soft dough forms, then knead for 3 minutes.
Divide into four balls, rest for 10 minutes, then roll each into a thin round.
Cook on a dry, hot pan or griddle for 2 to 3 minutes per side, until spotted brown.
recipes.safety: Cook until the bread is fully set through. If you have a wheat or gluten allergy, do not make this recipe.

recipes.name: Cultured milk, in the style of skyr
recipes.history: Soured and cultured milk products have long been part of the diet in Iceland and the Norse lands, kept for storage and for simple meals. This is a home version of a thick, soured milk.
ingredients: 2 tbsp plain yogurt with live cultures
steps: Heat the milk to 180°F (82°C), then cool it to about 110°F (43°C).
Whisk in the yogurt until smooth.
Keep warm for 8 hours in an oven with only the light on, or in a cooler packed with warm water.
Chill, then strain through cheesecloth for a thicker result.
recipes.safety: Use pasteurized milk and clean containers. Discard if it smells off or shows mould.
